# Incident Report: PCAP Forensic Analysis — 2024-09-04 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 172.17.0.99 | Source of all suspicious C2 traffic; consistent across ARP, DHCP, NBNS |
| MAC | 18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4 | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==172.17.0.99`), matches Ethernet source on all frames from .99, matches DHCP client MAC |
| Hostname | DESKTOP-RNVO9AT | DHCP option 12 hostname, NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` records, DNS query `DESKTOP-RNVO9AT.bepositive.com` |
| Logged-in user | afletcher (domain BEPOSITIVE, AD domain bepositive.com) | Kerberos `CNameString=afletcher` in AS-REQ from 172.17.0.99; TCP stream follow of the Kerberos exchange (tcp.stream 10) shows plaintext principal `afletcher@BEPOSITIVE.COM` |

Domain environment: AD domain `bepositive.com`, domain controller `WIN-CTL9XBQ9Y19` at 172.17.0.17 (MAC 00:23:ae:50:ba:fd). Gateway 172.17.0.1.

## Malware Family

**Koi Stealer** (Win32/Koi Stealer). **Attribution: signature-confirmed.**

The provided Suricata alert export contains a direct hit: `ETPRO TROJAN Win32/Koi Stealer CnC Checkin (POST) M2`, 48 occurrences, on the flow 172.17.0.99 → 79.124.78.197:80. This is corroborated behaviorally: the pcap shows 48 near-identical `POST /foots.php` requests to the bare-IP host 79.124.78.197, spaced roughly 60–95 seconds apart (classic beacon interval), all using the same spoofed legacy-IE User-Agent string. TCP stream follow of one checkin (tcp.stream 48) shows the request body format `101|<GUID>|<token>|<base64-like blob>` — a structured stealer checkin, not a normal web request — sent as `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`.

## Delivery Chain

- At t=153.3s the host opens a TLS session (SNI `www.bellantonicioccolato.it`, resolving to 46.254.34.201, an Italian chocolate-shop domain, almost certainly a compromised legitimate site used for payload staging) and pulls down ~701 KB.
- Two seconds later, at t=155.9s, the first `POST /foots.php` C2 checkin to 79.124.78.197 begins, and beaconing continues for the rest of the capture (~57 minutes).
- The tight timing correlation (payload pull → immediate C2 activation) strongly indicates 46.254.34.201/www.bellantonicioccolato.it was the payload delivery point, but the session is TLS-encrypted, so the exact download URL and the payload itself could not be recovered from this capture — no executable file or hash could be extracted.
- A gate-style exchange was also observed in plaintext HTTP: `GET /index.php?id=&subid=qIOuKk7U` to 79.124.78.197 returned `HckDcK0czXjaq48jVHNn|qIOuKk7U|http://79.124.78.197/index.php|` — a bot ID, the same subid token used in the request, and a callback URL — followed by a `POST /index.php` whose response body is a small opaque binary blob (105 bytes), consistent with a loader/config fetch preceding steady-state C2 beaconing.

## Benign / Noise Context (not IOCs)

The alert export also flags `ET POLICY Reserved Internal IP Traffic` (172.17.0.99↔172.17.0.17 DNS, normal internal DNS), `ET INFO Potentially unsafe SMBv1 protocol in use`, `GPL NETBIOS SMB Session Setup NTMLSSP unicode asn1 overflow attempt`, `GPL NETBIOS SMB IPC$ unicode share access`, `GPL NETBIOS SMB SMB_COM_TRANSACTION Max Data Count of 0 DOS Attempt`, and `GPL RPC kerberos principal name overflow TCP` — all between 172.17.0.99 and the domain controller 172.17.0.17. These are generic, decade-old GPL rules that routinely misfire on ordinary Windows domain-join SMB/Kerberos authentication traffic; the pcap shows this traffic is standard AD auth (SMB session setup, IPC$ share connect, Kerberos AS-REQ), not exploitation. Treated as noise, not compromise indicators.

Microsoft/Windows telemetry and update domains (`*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `oneclient.sfx.ms`, MSN/Bing content domains, `client.wns.windows.com`) and the Adobe ARM check (`acroipm2.adobe.com/assets/Owner/arm/ProcessMAU.txt`) are normal OS/application background activity.

## Indicators of Compromise
